role: Independent expert, production-plan.md section 5 steps 2 and 3 (blind solve, key check). Coach only; never published.
method: Each item was loaded from tools/mock/data/full-mocks.js with the pipeline loader (the vm window context build.mjs uses) and shown as served: stem and the five choices in bank order (tools/mock/full.js does not shuffle). No figure or structure is served on any of the 24.
Answers, reasoning, concept, misconceptions and confidence were written to a draft before any key was read; the key comparison ran after, by exact choice text.
Numbers recomputed in python (Hardy-Weinberg root, meiosis chromatid counts). RDKit 2026.09.1 was available; no item serves a SMILES, so there was nothing to check.
Families come from the closed list in scripts/explainers/families.js; missType follows the family. They are suggestions for the writer, who decides.
Bank why and trap notes were read only after the key check, to flag copy the writer should not lift; nothing in the bank was edited.

process.note: The first extraction pass hid the key and the why but printed the bank traps field, which is shown only in the post-test review and holds null at the key's index. That output was on screen before the draft was written. The extractor was then fixed to hide traps and blind.json rebuilt. All 24 are standard DAT Bio recall or concept items with one defensible answer each, solved by the reasoning recorded; still, Thomas should read this pass as not fully blind. A second blind solve by another agent would restore full independence if wanted.

summary.line: All 24 keys agree with the blind solve; no key dispute raised. Four bank-copy notes and one letter citation passed to the writer.

expert.answer: Ascomycota
expert.concept: Fungal phyla by their spore-making structure: yeasts like Saccharomyces are sac fungi (ascus).
reasoning: Name the defining structure: Saccharomyces makes its sexual spores (ascospores) inside a sac, the ascus.
The ascus is what defines Ascomycota, the sac fungi, which also includes Penicillium, morels and Neurospora.
Being single celled does not move yeast to another phylum; budding yeast is a sac fungus that lives as one cell.

misconceptions.choice: Zygomycota
misconceptions.pull: The "baker" and "bread" link pulls toward the bread mold Rhizopus, which is a zygomycete; the bread mold, not the bread yeast.

misconceptions.choice: Basidiomycota
misconceptions.pull: The best-known fungi (mushrooms, rusts, smuts) are club fungi, so a student who thinks "fungus = mushroom" lands here.

misconceptions.choice: Glomeromycota
misconceptions.pull: Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi that live inside plant roots; a real phylum, but not free-living single cells.

misconceptions.choice: Chytridiomycota
misconceptions.pull: Chytrids are often single celled too, which pulls a student who sorts by "unicellular", but they are aquatic with flagellated spores.

key.text: Ascomycota

expert.answer: Flagellated spores
expert.concept: Chytrids are the only fungi with a flagellated, swimming stage (zoospores), a trace of the aquatic ancestor.
reasoning: List what all fungi share: heterotrophs by absorption, chitin cell walls, both sexual and asexual cycles.
Any choice that is true of fungi in general cannot set chytrids apart.
The one feature only chytrids carry is a motile spore with a single posterior flagellum.

misconceptions.choice: Photosynthesis
misconceptions.pull: No fungus photosynthesizes; this borrows a plant or algal trait.

misconceptions.choice: Cell walls built from cellulose instead of chitin
misconceptions.pull: Cellulose walls belong to plants and to the fungus-like water molds (oomycetes); chytrid walls are chitin like other fungi.

misconceptions.choice: Multicellularity
misconceptions.pull: Most chytrids are single celled or simple; multicellular bodies are the rule in molds and mushrooms, so this runs the other way.

misconceptions.choice: Asexual only
misconceptions.pull: Chytrids reproduce both sexually and asexually; "asexual only" pulls from the old "imperfect fungi" (deuteromycetes) idea.

key.text: Flagellated spores

expert.answer: N₂ to NH₃
expert.concept: Nitrogen fixation turns atmospheric N2 into ammonia (nitrogenase in bacteria such as Rhizobium); the other steps of the cycle start from fixed nitrogen.
reasoning: Start at the atmosphere: N2 has a triple bond almost nothing can use.
Fixation is the one step that breaks it, reducing N2 to NH3 (nitrogenase, in free-living and root-nodule bacteria).
Every other step in the choices starts from nitrogen that is already fixed, so it comes after.

misconceptions.choice: NH₃ to NO₃⁻
misconceptions.pull: This is nitrification, the next step (Nitrosomonas then Nitrobacter); the neighbor process in the cycle.

misconceptions.choice: NO₃⁻ to N₂
misconceptions.pull: Denitrification returns nitrogen to the air, the cycle run the other way from fixation.

misconceptions.choice: NH₄⁺ to amino acids in plant tissue
misconceptions.pull: Assimilation: the plant building fixed nitrogen into its own molecules, a later step.

misconceptions.choice: Organic to inorganic
misconceptions.pull: Ammonification (decomposition) releases nitrogen already in living matter; fixation brings new nitrogen in from N2.

key.text: N₂ to NH₃

expert.answer: Trophic cascade; secondary-consumer numbers decline, primary consumers rebound, producer biomass decreases
expert.concept: Trophic cascade: adding a top predator flips each level below it in turn (down, up, down).
reasoning: Trace the arrows down from the new predator: it eats the secondary consumers, so they decline.
With fewer secondary consumers, the primary consumers are released from predation and rebound.
More primary consumers graze harder, so producer biomass falls. The pattern alternates level by level.

misconceptions.choice: Trophic cascade; secondary-consumer numbers decline, primary consumers also decline, producer biomass INCREASES
misconceptions.pull: Right that a cascade starts and secondary consumers decline, but the primary consumers would rise once their predator falls; this skips the alternation.

misconceptions.choice: No effect; the new predator only eats producers
misconceptions.pull: A plant eater is a primary consumer by definition; a tertiary consumer eats secondary consumers, so this describes a different trophic role.

misconceptions.choice: Loss of primary consumers across the food web
misconceptions.pull: Moves the effect a secondary consumer has (eating herbivores) onto the new top predator, which eats the secondary consumers instead.

misconceptions.choice: Linear decline in all populations
misconceptions.pull: Stops at "a predator lowers numbers" and applies it to every level without tracing the chain; the effects alternate down, up, down.

key.text: Trophic cascade; secondary-consumer numbers decline, primary consumers rebound, producer biomass decreases

expert.concept: Hardy-Weinberg: for a recessive trait the affected fraction is q^2, so q is its square root.
reasoning: Name what the stem gives: affected individuals of a recessive disorder are q^2, so q^2 = 1/10,000.
Take the square root: 10,000 is 100 x 100, so q = 1/100 = 0.01.
Check: 0.01 squared is 0.0001, one in ten thousand.

misconceptions.pull: This is q^2, the affected fraction the stem already gives; the square-root step is missing.
A power-of-ten slip between q^2 and q; squaring it gives one in a million, not one in ten thousand.
Off by a power of ten in the other direction; 0.1 squared is 1/100, a disorder in one person per hundred.
That is p, the dominant allele frequency (1 - q), a true value for the other allele.

expert.answer: Stabilizing
expert.concept: Stabilizing selection removes both extremes and keeps the mean in place (human birth weight is the textbook case).
reasoning: Read the two clues: values cluster tightly at the middle, and the average does not move over time.
Selection against both tails narrows the spread without shifting the mean: that is stabilizing selection.
Very small and very large infants both had lower survival, so intermediate weight is favored.

misconceptions.choice: Directional
misconceptions.pull: Directional selection shifts the mean one way over generations; the stem says the average held still.

misconceptions.choice: Drift
misconceptions.pull: Drift is random change in allele frequency, not selection, and it would not hold a trait tightly at one value.

misconceptions.choice: Sexual selection acting on a trait that improves mating success
misconceptions.pull: Sexual selection acts on traits for winning mates; birth weight acts on infant survival, a different pressure.

misconceptions.choice: Disruptive
misconceptions.pull: Disruptive selection favors both extremes over the middle, the opposite of a tight cluster at the mean.

key.text: Stabilizing

expert.answer: 16 at metaphase I and 8 at metaphase II
expert.concept: Chromatid counting in meiosis: replication doubles chromatids before meiosis I; meiosis I halves the chromosome number while sister chromatids stay joined until anaphase II.
reasoning: Start with 2n = 8 chromosomes. DNA replicates once in S phase, so at metaphase I there are 8 chromosomes and 16 chromatids.
Meiosis I separates homologs, so each daughter cell gets 4 chromosomes, each still two sister chromatids.
At metaphase II the sisters are still joined: 4 chromosomes x 2 = 8 chromatids.

misconceptions.choice: 16 at metaphase I and 16 at metaphase II
misconceptions.pull: Leaves out the reduction in meiosis I; a metaphase II cell holds half the DNA of a metaphase I cell.

misconceptions.choice: 32 at metaphase I and 16 at metaphase II
misconceptions.pull: Doubles twice: treats the diploid number 8 as already replicated and doubles it again; DNA is copied once.

misconceptions.choice: 8 at metaphase I and 4 at metaphase II
misconceptions.pull: Counts chromosomes instead of chromatids, at both stages.

misconceptions.choice: 16 at metaphase I and 4 at metaphase II
misconceptions.pull: Metaphase I is right in chromatids, but metaphase II switches to counting chromosomes (4) instead of chromatids (8).

key.text: 16 at metaphase I and 8 at metaphase II

expert.answer: Trisomies
expert.concept: About half of first-trimester losses carry a chromosomal error, and autosomal trisomies (nondisjunction, often maternal meiosis I) are the largest single class.
reasoning: Ask what kind of error is large enough to stop development early: a whole extra or missing chromosome, not a single base change.
Among chromosomally abnormal early losses, autosomal trisomies are the most common class (trisomy 16 leads), well ahead of monosomy X and triploidy.
Trisomies come from nondisjunction in meiosis, which ties the item to its meiosis subtopic.

misconceptions.choice: Translocations
misconceptions.pull: Unbalanced translocations do cause loss (often from a balanced carrier parent), but they are a much smaller share than trisomies.

misconceptions.choice: Point mutations
misconceptions.pull: A single base change usually affects one protein; it is not the usual cause of early loss.

misconceptions.choice: Inversions
misconceptions.pull: An inversion keeps all of the genetic material, so carriers are often unaffected; it is a structural change with little dosage effect.

misconceptions.choice: Triploidy, from two sperm fertilizing one egg
misconceptions.pull: Triploidy is a real and common cause (dispermy is its usual origin), but it accounts for fewer losses than the autosomal trisomies as a group.

key.text: Trisomies

expert.answer: Electron transport continues while ATP synthesis collapses
expert.concept: Uncoupling: the proton gradient links electron transport to ATP synthase; a proton leak cuts the link, so the chain keeps running while ATP synthesis stops.
reasoning: Put the gradient in the middle: electron transport pumps protons into the lumen, and ATP synthase spends that gradient to make ATP.
A membrane freely permeable to protons lets the gradient leak away, so ATP synthase has nothing to run on.
The carriers are not blocked; light still drives electrons from water to NADP+, and with no back-pressure they may even run faster.

misconceptions.choice: Both electron transport and ATP synthesis speed up together
misconceptions.pull: Electron transport can speed up with no gradient pushing back, but ATP synthesis cannot rise without the gradient.

misconceptions.choice: Water splitting stops while NADPH production continues
misconceptions.pull: NADPH production does continue, but it needs electrons from water splitting, which keeps going too.

misconceptions.choice: Electron transport halts while ATP synthesis continues
misconceptions.pull: Swaps the two effects: the leak hits the gradient, so ATP synthesis stops and the chain keeps going.

misconceptions.choice: The Calvin cycle speeds up because more protons reach the stroma
misconceptions.pull: Protons leaking to the stroma do no work, and the Calvin cycle slows because it loses its ATP supply.

key.text: Electron transport continues while ATP synthesis collapses

notes: Over longer times NADP+ would run short and the chain would slow; the stem asks the immediate effect, so the key holds.

expert.answer: Two molecules of the three carbon acid 3-PGA
expert.concept: Carbon fixation: RuBisCO adds CO2 to RuBP (5C) to make an unstable 6C intermediate that splits at once into two 3-PGA (3C).
reasoning: Count carbons: 5 from RuBP plus 1 from CO2 makes 6.
That 6-carbon intermediate is unstable and splits at once into two 3-carbon molecules of 3-PGA.
G3P comes later, after ATP and NADPH reduce 3-PGA.

misconceptions.choice: One two carbon fragment and one three carbon acid
misconceptions.pull: This is the oxygenase reaction (photorespiration): RuBisCO adds O2 and makes 2-phosphoglycolate plus one 3-PGA.

misconceptions.choice: Two molecules of G3P, ready to leave the cycle
misconceptions.pull: G3P is made after the reduction steps that spend ATP and NADPH; it is not the first product.

misconceptions.choice: One stable six carbon sugar that leaves the cycle
misconceptions.pull: The 6-carbon intermediate is real but unstable; it splits before anything leaves.

misconceptions.choice: One four carbon oxaloacetate
misconceptions.pull: Oxaloacetate is the first product of PEP carboxylase in C4 and CAM plants, a different enzyme.

key.text: Two molecules of the three carbon acid 3-PGA

expert.answer: RuBP falls and 3-PGA rises
expert.concept: Calvin cycle supply and demand: darkness stops ATP and NADPH, so 3-PGA is still made but no longer reduced, and RuBP is still used but no longer rebuilt.
reasoning: Split the cycle at RuBisCO: fixation (RuBP + CO2 to 3-PGA) needs no ATP; reducing 3-PGA and rebuilding RuBP both need ATP (and NADPH for the reduction).
In the dark, ATP and NADPH run out within seconds, so 3-PGA stops being used and piles up.
RuBisCO keeps consuming RuBP for a few seconds, and without ATP none is rebuilt, so RuBP falls.

misconceptions.choice: RuBP rises and 3-PGA falls
misconceptions.pull: This is the pattern when CO2 is cut off with the light on: fixation stops, RuBP piles up, 3-PGA drains.

misconceptions.choice: Both rise together
misconceptions.pull: 3-PGA does rise, but RuBP is still being consumed and is no longer rebuilt, so it cannot rise.

misconceptions.choice: Both fall immediately
misconceptions.pull: RuBP does fall, but fixation keeps running briefly, so 3-PGA builds up rather than drops.

misconceptions.choice: Neither changes until the leaf runs out of carbon dioxide
misconceptions.pull: Reads the "dark reactions" name literally; the Calvin cycle depends on ATP and NADPH from the light reactions, so darkness shows within seconds.

key.text: RuBP falls and 3-PGA rises

expert.answer: ADP and NADP+
expert.concept: The light reactions and the Calvin cycle trade carriers: ATP and NADPH go to the stroma, ADP (plus Pi) and NADP+ come back to be recharged.
reasoning: Here is the loop: the light reactions charge carriers, the Calvin cycle spends them.
Spent ATP becomes ADP (plus phosphate); spent NADPH becomes NADP+.
Those empty carriers go back to the thylakoid to be recharged.

misconceptions.choice: Carbon dioxide and G3P
misconceptions.pull: CO2 is the input from the air and G3P is the output; neither returns to the thylakoid.

misconceptions.choice: Oxygen and water
misconceptions.pull: O2 is a byproduct of water splitting at the thylakoid and water is its input; neither is sent back by the Calvin cycle.

misconceptions.choice: ATP and NADPH
misconceptions.pull: These are the charged carriers that arrive at the Calvin cycle; the item asks for the direction back.

misconceptions.choice: Glucose and phosphate
misconceptions.pull: Glucose is built from G3P outside the cycle and is an end product, not a returned carrier.

key.text: ADP and NADP+

expert.answer: From the lumen into the stroma, with the ATP appearing in the stroma
expert.concept: Chemiosmosis in the chloroplast: protons pumped into the lumen flow back down their gradient through ATP synthase, whose catalytic head faces the stroma, where the Calvin cycle uses the ATP.
reasoning: Find where protons pile up: water splitting and the cytochrome b6f complex load protons into the thylakoid lumen.
Protons flow downhill through ATP synthase, out of the lumen and into the stroma.
The synthase head sticks into the stroma, so ATP is released there, right where the Calvin cycle spends it.

misconceptions.choice: From the stroma into the lumen, with the ATP appearing in the lumen
misconceptions.pull: Both parts run the other way: that is the pumping direction, and the lumen is not where ATP is made.

misconceptions.choice: From the cytosol into the stroma, with the ATP appearing in the stroma
misconceptions.pull: The cytosol is outside the chloroplast; this borrows an outer-to-inner layout like the mitochondrion (intermembrane space to matrix).

misconceptions.choice: From the lumen into the stroma, with the ATP appearing in the lumen
misconceptions.pull: The proton direction is right, but the catalytic head faces the stroma, so ATP appears in the stroma.

misconceptions.choice: From the stroma into the lumen, with the ATP appearing in the stroma
misconceptions.pull: ATP does appear in the stroma, but protons move through the synthase out of the lumen, not into it.

key.text: From the lumen into the stroma, with the ATP appearing in the stroma

expert.answer: The extrinsic pathway, working through a death receptor, activating caspase-8
expert.concept: Two routes to apoptosis: extrinsic (a death receptor such as Fas at the membrane, initiator caspase-8) and intrinsic (mitochondrial cytochrome c, apoptosome, caspase-9); both converge on executioner caspase-3.
reasoning: Spot the signal source: Fas ligand on the T cell binds Fas, a death receptor on the target surface. A signal from outside the cell is the extrinsic pathway.
Fas clusters, recruits the adaptor FADD and procaspase-8 (the DISC), and caspase-8 is the first caspase switched on.
Caspase-8 then activates executioner caspases such as caspase-3; caspase-9 belongs to the mitochondrial route.

misconceptions.choice: The extrinsic pathway, working through cytochrome c release, activating caspase-9
misconceptions.pull: The pathway name is right, but cytochrome c and caspase-9 belong to the intrinsic route.

misconceptions.choice: Neither pathway, since Fas binding produces necrosis rather than apoptosis
misconceptions.pull: Fas signaling is a controlled caspase program with the hallmarks of apoptosis; necrosis is uncontrolled swelling and rupture.

misconceptions.choice: The intrinsic pathway, working through a death receptor, activating caspase-3 first
misconceptions.pull: A death receptor is right, but that makes it extrinsic, and caspase-3 is an executioner activated after the initiator.

misconceptions.choice: The intrinsic pathway, working through the mitochondrion, activating caspase-9
misconceptions.pull: A true description of the other pathway, which starts from damage inside the cell.

key.text: The extrinsic pathway, working through a death receptor, activating caspase-8

expert.answer: Metaphase, held by balanced pull from microtubules reaching to each pole
expert.concept: Metaphase: every chromosome sits on the metaphase plate with its sister kinetochores attached to microtubules from opposite poles, held in place by balanced tension.
reasoning: Read the picture in the stem: one tight line across the middle is the metaphase plate.
"Gripped from both sides" is bi-orientation: each sister kinetochore is bound by microtubules from the opposite pole.
The opposing pulls balance, which keeps the line in place until anaphase.

misconceptions.choice: Telophase, held by the two nuclear envelopes that are reassembling nearby
misconceptions.pull: In telophase the chromosomes sit at the two poles and envelopes re-form; a later step, not a line in the middle.

misconceptions.choice: Interphase, held by the cell plate that is forming across the equator
misconceptions.pull: Interphase chromatin is not condensed into visible chromosomes, and a cell plate belongs to plant cytokinesis.

misconceptions.choice: Prophase, held together by a nuclear envelope that has not yet broken down
misconceptions.pull: Prophase chromosomes condense but are scattered in the nucleus with no spindle grip; an earlier step.

misconceptions.choice: Anaphase, held in place by the contractile ring forming around the equator
misconceptions.pull: In anaphase the chromatids move toward the poles, and the contractile ring belongs to animal cytokinesis.

key.text: Metaphase, held by balanced pull from microtubules reaching to each pole

expert.answer: Proteases, switched on by cleavage, initiator caspases activating executioner ones
expert.concept: Caspases are cysteine proteases made as inactive zymogens; initiator caspases (8, 9) cleave and activate executioner caspases (3, 6, 7), which take the cell apart.
reasoning: Name the enzyme family: caspases are proteases (cysteine-dependent, cutting after aspartate).
They sit as inactive procaspases and are switched on by cleavage, so one active caspase can activate many others.
Initiators (caspase-8 or 9) activate executioners (caspase-3, 6, 7), the cascade the stem describes.

misconceptions.choice: Nucleases, activated by a calcium surge, which cut the plasma membrane into blebs
misconceptions.pull: A DNase (CAD) does fragment DNA late in apoptosis, but it is downstream of caspases, and a nuclease cannot cut membrane.

misconceptions.choice: Phosphatases, activated by cytochrome c, which strip phosphate off the mitotic spindle
misconceptions.pull: Cytochrome c is real in apoptosis, but it triggers a protease cascade (via the apoptosome), not phosphatases.

misconceptions.choice: Kinases, activated by cyclin binding, which phosphorylate the nuclear lamins
misconceptions.pull: Cyclin-dependent kinases phosphorylate lamins to take the envelope apart in mitosis; a nearby process, not cell death.

misconceptions.choice: Ligases, activated by ATP binding, which crosslink the cytoskeleton into a rigid mesh
misconceptions.pull: Ligases join molecules; apoptosis takes cell structures apart, the opposite job.

key.text: Proteases, switched on by cleavage, initiator caspases activating executioner ones

expert.answer: Allantois
expert.concept: Amniote egg membranes and their jobs: the allantois stores nitrogenous waste (uric acid) and, fused with the chorion, does gas exchange.
reasoning: List the four extraembryonic membranes with one job each: amnion cushions, yolk sac feeds, chorion exchanges gas, allantois stores waste.
A bird embryo in a sealed shell cannot flush waste, so it stores uric acid in the allantois.
In mammals the allantois becomes part of the umbilical cord vessels; in birds it is the waste sac.

misconceptions.choice: Chorion
misconceptions.pull: The chorion lines the shell and handles gas exchange (with the allantois), but stores no waste.

misconceptions.choice: The albumen surrounding the embryo
misconceptions.pull: Albumen is egg white, a water and protein supply from the hen, not an embryonic membrane.

misconceptions.choice: Amnion
misconceptions.pull: The amnion holds fluid that cushions the embryo and keeps it moist.

misconceptions.choice: Yolk sac
misconceptions.pull: The yolk sac supplies food from the yolk.

expert.answer: Ectoderm
expert.concept: Germ layer fates: the lens forms from surface ectoderm (the lens placode), induced by the optic vesicle, which itself grows out of the neural tube.
reasoning: Trace the induction: the optic vesicle (neural tube) grows out and touches the surface ectoderm.
That contact induces the surface ectoderm to thicken into the lens placode, which becomes the lens.
Ectoderm builds the outer layer and the nervous system; the lens is surface ectoderm.

misconceptions.choice: Neural crest
misconceptions.pull: Neural crest builds parts of the eye (corneal stroma and endothelium, much of the iris stroma), but not the lens.

misconceptions.choice: Mesoderm and neural crest together
misconceptions.pull: Both supply eye structures (muscles, vessels, corneal layers), but neither forms the lens.

misconceptions.choice: Mesoderm
misconceptions.pull: Head mesoderm forms the extraocular muscles and vessels of the eye, not the lens.

misconceptions.choice: Endoderm
misconceptions.pull: Endoderm lines the gut and its glands; it never reaches the eye.

key.text: Ectoderm

expert.answer: ATP
expert.concept: Second messengers by substrate: adenylyl cyclase cyclizes ATP into cAMP (releasing pyrophosphate); guanylyl cyclase does the same with GTP.
reasoning: Read the name: adenylyl means the adenine nucleotide, and cAMP is cyclic adenosine monophosphate.
The enzyme takes ATP, removes pyrophosphate, and closes the ring to make cAMP.
The G-protein (GTP) story stays upstream: Gs-GTP activates the enzyme, but its substrate is ATP.

misconceptions.choice: PIP2
misconceptions.pull: PIP2 is the substrate of phospholipase C, which makes IP3 and DAG, a neighbor pathway.

misconceptions.choice: GTP
misconceptions.pull: GTP is the substrate of guanylyl cyclase (making cGMP), and GTP on Gs activates adenylyl cyclase, which pulls students here.

misconceptions.choice: Phosphocreatine
misconceptions.pull: A muscle phosphate reserve for regenerating ATP, not a signaling substrate.

misconceptions.choice: Cholesterol
misconceptions.pull: Cholesterol is the precursor of steroid hormones, not of a cyclic nucleotide.

key.text: ATP

expert.answer: Adds phosphate groups to tyrosines on its own cytoplasmic tails
expert.concept: The insulin receptor is a receptor tyrosine kinase: binding switches on its kinase, which autophosphorylates tyrosines on the beta subunits and then docks IRS proteins.
reasoning: Name the receptor class: insulin uses a receptor tyrosine kinase.
Binding to the outer alpha subunits changes the shape of the dimer, and the beta subunits phosphorylate each other on tyrosines (autophosphorylation).
Those phosphotyrosines recruit IRS proteins, which carry the signal on (PI3K to Akt to GLUT4 moving to the membrane).

misconceptions.choice: Cleaves PIP2 into IP3 and DAG
misconceptions.pull: That is phospholipase C, downstream of Gq receptors (and some RTKs), not the first act of the insulin receptor.

misconceptions.choice: Carries insulin with it into the nucleus
misconceptions.pull: Moving with the hormone to the nucleus is how lipid-soluble steroid hormones work; insulin is a peptide acting at the surface.

misconceptions.choice: Opens as an ion channel and lets sodium in
misconceptions.pull: Ligand-gated ion channels (for example the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor) do this; a different receptor class.

misconceptions.choice: Exchanges GDP for GTP on an attached G protein at the inner surface
misconceptions.pull: That is the job of a G-protein-coupled receptor, the other big surface receptor class.

key.text: Adds phosphate groups to tyrosines on its own cytoplasmic tails

items.bankTopic: The membrane and what crosses it

expert.answer: A gap junction
expert.concept: Cell junctions by job: gap junctions (connexon channels) link cytoplasms, which lets heart cells pass the action potential (in the intercalated discs).
reasoning: Match the job: "pass directly from cytoplasm to cytoplasm" means a channel through both membranes.
In animal cells that channel is the gap junction, built from connexons.
Cardiac cells use gap junctions in the intercalated discs so the action potential spreads cell to cell.

misconceptions.choice: A hemidesmosome
misconceptions.pull: Hemidesmosomes anchor a cell to the basement membrane below it, not to another cell.

misconceptions.choice: A tight junction
misconceptions.pull: Tight junctions seal the space between cells to block leaks; they do not join cytoplasms.

misconceptions.choice: A plasmodesma
misconceptions.pull: Plasmodesmata do link cytoplasms, but in plant cells; cardiac muscle is animal tissue.

misconceptions.choice: A desmosome
misconceptions.pull: Desmosomes are mechanical rivets (also in intercalated discs) that hold cells together under stress, with no channel.

key.text: A gap junction

items.bankTopic: The membrane and what crosses it

expert.answer: The sodium gradient that powers the cotransporter runs down
expert.concept: Secondary active transport: the sodium glucose cotransporter uses the sodium gradient that the Na+/K+ ATPase builds; block the pump and the gradient, and then glucose uptake, fade over minutes.
reasoning: Trace the energy: the Na+/K+ ATPase spends ATP to keep inside sodium low.
The cotransporter lets sodium run down that gradient and drags glucose in with it, uphill.
Block the pump and sodium leaks in until the gradient is gone, so glucose uptake falls within minutes.

misconceptions.choice: The cotransporter needs ATP, and the drug has cut off its supply
misconceptions.pull: True of the pump (primary active transport); the cotransporter itself never hydrolyzes ATP.

misconceptions.choice: The apical membrane depolarizes, which closes the carrier
misconceptions.pull: Depolarization does happen and trims the driving force on this electrogenic carrier, but it does not close the carrier; the lost sodium gradient is the main cause.

misconceptions.choice: The drug binds the glucose carrier directly and jams its binding site
misconceptions.pull: The stem says the drug blocks the pump; the minutes-long delay fits a gradient running down, not direct block of the carrier.

misconceptions.choice: Glucose is no longer phosphorylated once it arrives inside the cell
misconceptions.pull: Phosphorylation by hexokinase traps glucose in many cells, but it is not the energy source for this carrier.

key.text: The sodium gradient that powers the cotransporter runs down

items.bankTopic: The membrane and what crosses it

expert.answer: The carrier proteins are saturated, so transport has a ceiling
expert.concept: Carrier-mediated transport saturates (Vmax-like curve) because there are a fixed number of carriers; simple diffusion rises in a straight line with no ceiling.
reasoning: Look at the shape: uptake rises, then levels off at a maximum.
A ceiling means a limited number of something; here, the glucose carriers (GLUT proteins).
Once every carrier is busy, more outside glucose cannot raise the rate.

misconceptions.choice: Glucose is entering by simple diffusion straight through the lipid bilayer
misconceptions.pull: Simple diffusion rises in a straight line with concentration and never levels off; the plateau points the other way.

misconceptions.choice: The cell has begun pumping glucose back out at an equal rate
misconceptions.pull: Nothing in the data shows efflux; the plateau is a limit on entry, not a second flow out.

misconceptions.choice: Glucose crossing has switched over to active transport
misconceptions.pull: Active carriers saturate too, so the plateau does not show a change of mode; entry down the gradient needs no energy.

misconceptions.choice: The membrane became impermeable to glucose at high concentration
misconceptions.pull: Membranes do not switch permeability off with concentration; uptake stays at its maximum, it does not drop to zero.

key.text: The carrier proteins are saturated, so transport has a ceiling

items.bankTopic: The membrane and what crosses it

expert.answer: IP3 and DAG, and IP3 releases calcium from the smooth endoplasmic reticulum
expert.concept: The phospholipase C pathway: PIP2 splits into IP3 (water soluble, opens ER calcium channels) and DAG (stays in the membrane, activates protein kinase C with calcium).
reasoning: Name the cut: phospholipase C splits the membrane lipid PIP2 into IP3 and DAG.
Sort by solubility: IP3 is water soluble and diffuses through the cytosol; DAG is lipid and stays in the membrane.
IP3 opens calcium channels on the smooth ER (the sarcoplasmic reticulum in muscle), and the calcium drives smooth muscle contraction.

misconceptions.choice: cAMP and cGMP, and cAMP activates protein kinase A in the cytoplasm of the cell
misconceptions.pull: cAMP and cGMP come from the two cyclases; the PKA link is true but belongs to the adenylyl cyclase pathway.

misconceptions.choice: IP3 and DAG, and IP3 stays in the membrane to activate protein kinase C
misconceptions.pull: The pair is right, but the roles are swapped: DAG stays in the membrane for PKC, IP3 travels.

misconceptions.choice: DAG and calcium, and DAG travels to the nucleus to bind DNA
misconceptions.pull: DAG is one product, but calcium is released downstream (not a PLC product), and DAG stays in the membrane, it does not bind DNA.

misconceptions.choice: cAMP and calcium, and cAMP opens calcium channels in the nucleus
misconceptions.pull: cAMP comes from adenylyl cyclase, not PLC, and the calcium store IP3 taps is the ER, not the nucleus.

key.text: IP3 and DAG, and IP3 releases calcium from the smooth endoplasmic reticulum
